glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
kismat-maria-mosque.desc: The Kismat Maria Mosque stands in Maria village in Durgapur upazila and is thought to date from around 1500. It is a small rectangular building with three entrances, protected by the Department of Archaeology. To its south is a little two-storey structure that villagers call the Bibir Ghor. Few outsiders come here, and the mosque is still part of village life, filling up for Friday prayers.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Rajshahi to Durgapur, then a local auto-rickshaw to Maria village.
Good to know
Avoid visiting during prayer times, and ask before photographing people.

rajshahi-central-park-zoo.desc: Shaheed A.H.M. Qamaruzzaman Central Park covers about 33 acres beside the Padma, on land that was a horse racecourse in British times. It opened as a public park in 1972, and a zoo was added in 1983. Inside are a lake with paddle boats, shaded walking paths, children's rides and a small hill with a view over the river. The zoo keeps deer, monkeys, crocodiles, birds and a few big animals.
blocks: How to get there
It is in the west of the city near the Padma; take a rickshaw or auto-rickshaw and ask for 'Chiriyakhana'.
Good to know
Weekdays are calmer; on Fridays and Eid holidays the park is packed.

glance: Roughly 250–450 BDT per kg for good patali gur
Village markets in Bagha, Charghat and Puthia during winter
rajshahi-khejur-gur.desc: From late October, gachhis (sap collectors) in Bagha, Charghat and Puthia climb date palms each evening to tap the trunks and hang clay pots. At dawn the sap is drunk fresh or boiled in wide pans over wood fires until it thickens into liquid jhola gur or sets into solid patali cakes. The flavour is deep and caramel-like, and it goes into winter pithas and payesh. Visiting a boiling yard on a misty morning is a classic Rajshahi winter experience.
blocks: Good to know
Buy from producers you can see boiling the sap; some market gur is mixed with sugar. Health officials advise against drinking raw sap because of Nipah virus risk.

glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
kheturi-dham.desc: Kheturi Dham at Premtali in Godagari upazila is tied to Narottam Das Thakur, a Gaudiya Vaishnav saint of the 16th century who came from this area. Devotees believe he had a spiritual awakening while bathing in the Padma at Premtali. The Kheturi festival, first held here more than four centuries ago, still draws Vaishnav devotees from many districts. Outside festival days the place is quiet, with temples close to the river.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or CNG from Rajshahi towards Godagari and get off at Premtali.
Good to know
The yearly festival is the liveliest time, but also very crowded. Remove shoes in the temple areas.

rajshahi-padma-riverfront.desc: Rajshahi's southern edge runs along a raised embankment above the Padma, and stretches of it have been turned into walkways and small parks. In the evening families and students come to stroll, eat street snacks and watch the sun drop over the river. In the dry season sandbanks appear in the middle of the channel, and boatmen offer short rides out to them. The breeze makes it the best place in the city on a warm afternoon.
blocks: How to get there
Take a rickshaw or auto-rickshaw to the T-Badh or Padma Garden areas in the city.
Good to know
Late afternoon is best. Agree on a price before taking a boat and avoid going out when the river is high.

glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
puthia-temple-complex.desc: Puthia was the seat of a wealthy zamindar family, and the temples they built from the 18th and 19th centuries still stand around a set of large ponds. The tall Shiva Temple rises in tiers beside Shiv Sagar, while the smaller Govinda and Jagannath temples are covered in fine terracotta panels showing gods, battles and village life. The family palace, the Puthia Rajbari, faces an open field nearby. It is easy to walk between all the main buildings in a morning.
blocks: How to get there
Puthia is about 30 km east of Rajshahi city on the Rajshahi–Natore highway; buses drop you at Puthia bus stand, a short rickshaw ride from the temples.
Good to know
Go in the morning for soft light on the terracotta. Some temples are active places of worship, so remove shoes where asked.

glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
boro-kuthi-rajshahi.desc: Boro Kuthi is a plain, solid two-storey building that Dutch traders put up on the bank of the Padma in the early 1700s for their silk and indigo business. When the Dutch left after 1757 it passed to the East India Company, and in 1833 it was sold to Robert Watson and Company. After 1947 it served as a government supply depot, and from 1953 it was the first administrative office of the new Rajshahi University. It is now in the care of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, with plans to turn it into a museum.
blocks: How to get there
It sits on the riverfront just south of Rajshahi College in the city centre; any rickshaw or auto-rickshaw will take you.
Good to know
The building is often locked, so you may only see it from outside. Pair it with an evening walk along the Padma embankment right next to it.

varendra-research-museum.desc: Founded in 1910 by local patrons and now run by Rajshahi University, the museum holds a rich collection of stone and bronze sculpture from the Pala and Sena periods. Galleries also display terracotta plaques, coins, inscriptions and old manuscripts gathered from across North Bengal. The red-brick building itself blends local and colonial styles. It is a good place to understand the history behind Paharpur, Mahasthangarh and other sites in the region.
blocks: How to get there
The museum is in central Rajshahi near Shaheb Bazar; any rickshaw driver will know it.
Good to know
Check the weekly closing day before you go. Photography rules can change, so ask at the desk.

glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
bagha-mosque.desc: Built in the early 1500s during the Bengal Sultanate, the Bagha Mosque is a compact brick building topped by ten small domes. Its walls carry delicate terracotta panels of flowers and vines, many of them still crisp. The mosque stands in a quiet compound with a large pond and the shrine of a local saint. Few travellers make the trip out, so you can usually look around in peace.
blocks: How to get there
Bagha is about 40 km south-east of Rajshahi city; take a bus or CNG towards Bagha upazila and ask for the old mosque.
Good to know
It is an active mosque, so dress modestly and avoid prayer times. Combine with the mango orchards around Bagha in summer.

glance: Old sweet shops in central Rajshahi city, such as Rajshahi Mistanna Bhandar
rajshahi-roshkodom.desc: Roshkodom is a sweet Rajshahi is proud of. A soft ball of milk sweet is rolled in large white sugar beads until it looks like the round kadam flower it is named after. It is drier than syrup sweets, which makes it easy to carry home. Old sweet shops in the city, including the long-running Rajshahi Mistanna Bhandar, sell it alongside roshmalai, malai chop and chhana sweets.

glance: 265 km to Rajshahi by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
rajshahi-university-campus.desc: Rajshahi University, founded in 1953, has a large, leafy campus at Motihar on the eastern side of the city. Wide roads lined with old trees run between the halls and faculty buildings, and students fill the tea stalls and open fields in the evening. Visitors come to see the Shabash Bangladesh sculpture honouring the Liberation War and the Shaheed Smriti Sangrahashala, a museum of 1971. Near the main gate stands Motihar Kuthi, an old colonial-era building.
blocks: How to get there
Take an auto-rickshaw or bus along the Rajshahi–Dhaka road to the university main gate (Binodpur or Kajla gate).
Good to know
Go in the late afternoon when the campus is lively. Respect class and exam areas, and check that the museum is open before you go.

rajshahi-silk.desc: Rajshahi has been the centre of Bangladesh's silk industry for generations, from mulberry cultivation and silkworm rearing to spinning and weaving. Rajshahi silk sarees are known for their soft sheen and are popular for weddings and festivals. Several workshops and showrooms in the Sapura area let visitors watch looms at work and buy directly. The craft has faced hard times but remains closely tied to the city's identity.
blocks: How to get there
Ask a rickshaw for the silk showrooms in Sapura, in the north-east of the city.
Good to know
Ask to see the weaving floor as well as the showroom. Check whether a fabric is pure silk or a blend before buying.

glance: Roughly 80–200 BDT per kg depending on variety and timing
Markets in Rajshahi city, and the orchard areas around Bagha and Charghat
rajshahi-mango.desc: Rajshahi has given its name to Bangladeshi mangoes, and the district's orchards produce well-loved varieties such as Gopalbhog, Khirsapat (Himsagar), Langra and the large, late Fazli. From late May to July, roadside markets fill with baskets and trucks loading fruit for the rest of the country. Eating a perfectly ripe Khirsapat straight from a local market is very different from a supermarket mango. Many orchards welcome visitors who ask politely.
blocks: Good to know
Early varieties like Gopalbhog arrive first; Langra and Fazli come later in the season.

glance: Roughly 100–250 BDT per person with rice or roti
Busy local eateries in central Rajshahi city, and the late-night hotels at Katakhali on the eastern edge of the city
rajshahi-kala-bhuna.desc: Kala bhuna is beef cooked down for hours with onion, garlic and plenty of spice until the gravy turns almost black and clings to the meat. The dish came from Chattogram, but Rajshahi has made its own name with it, and small eateries across the city cook it in big pots from early morning. Locals eat it with plain rice or roti, often late in the evening. A plate is one of the cheapest good meals in town.
blocks: Good to know
Go hungry and ask for roti if you want to taste the gravy properly.

shah-makhdum-dargah.desc: Shah Makhdum Ruposh was a Sufi from Baghdad who reached Bengal in the late 13th century and is remembered for spreading Islam across the Varendra region. His shrine, the dargah, stands in the old part of Rajshahi near the Padma, and the neighbourhood around it is still called Dargapara. Pilgrims come throughout the day to pray, and the place gets much busier during the yearly urs. Rajshahi's Shah Makhdum Airport carries his name.
blocks: How to get there
Take a rickshaw or auto-rickshaw to Dargapara in the city; it is close to the Padma riverfront.
Good to know
Dress modestly, take off your shoes where asked and keep your voice down. Women may have a separate area for prayer.

glance: Beside the Sub-Registry Office wall in the court area of Rajshahi city
hoba-ghosh-rosogolla.desc: Hoba Ghosh's grandfather began making rosogolla in Rajshahi around 1937, and Hoba Ghosh himself has carried it on for more than six decades. The stall has no signboard; it sits by the wall of the Sub-Registry Office near the court, where people who have just registered land buy a packet to share. The rosogolla is made from fresh chhana only, so it stays soft and light. Regulars sit on low stools and mop up the syrup with bread.
blocks: Good to know
There is no sign; ask anyone in the court area for Hoba Ghosh's rosogolla.
